diseases.hypertension: High blood pressure — your heart is working harder than it should to pump blood.
diseases.anxiety: Anxiety can cause persistent worry or fear and may affect daily life. A clinician can help assess symptoms and treatment options.
diseases.gastric: A general term for stomach-related discomfort; it does not identify one specific diagnosis.
diseases.diabetes mellitus: A condition where your body has trouble controlling blood sugar levels.
diseases.myocardial infarction: A heart attack — part of the heart muscle isn't getting enough blood.
diseases.hyperlipidemia: High levels of fat (cholesterol) in your blood.
diseases.anemia: Your blood doesn't have enough healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen well.
diseases.pneumonia: An infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs.
diseases.hypothyroidism: Your thyroid gland isn't making enough hormone, which can slow down your body.
diseases.hyperthyroidism: Your thyroid gland is making too much hormone, speeding up your body's processes.
diseases.osteoarthritis: Wear-and-tear damage to joint cartilage, causing pain and stiffness.
diseases.chronic kidney disease: Your kidneys are gradually losing their ability to filter waste from your blood.
diseases.asthma: A chronic condition that inflames and narrows airways, making breathing difficult at times.
diseases.fatty liver: An accumulation of extra fat in liver cells that warrants metabolic and lifestyle review.
diseases.jaundice: A yellowish tint of the skin or eyes caused by elevated bilirubin levels.
diseases.gout: A painful form of arthritis caused by uric acid crystal buildup in the joints.
diseases.gerd: Gastroesophageal reflux disease — stomach acid frequently flows back into the tube connecting your mouth and stomach.
diseases.cold: Common cold — a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract causing congestion, sneezing, and sore throat.
diseases.fever: Elevated body temperature often signaling the body's immune response to an infection.
diseases.cold and fever: Cold accompanied by fever — acute viral symptoms affecting body temperature and the respiratory tract.
diseases.common cold: A viral upper respiratory infection causing sneezing, sore throat, and nasal congestion.

medicines.metformin: A common medicine to help control blood sugar in diabetes.
medicines.atorvastatin: A medicine that lowers cholesterol levels in the blood.
medicines.amlodipine: A medicine that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure.
medicines.levothyroxine: A medicine that replaces thyroid hormone your body isn't making enough of.
medicines.paracetamol: A common pain reliever and fever reducer.
medicines.aspirin: A medicine used to reduce pain, fever, and to help prevent blood clots.
medicines.omeprazole: A medicine that reduces stomach acid, used for acid reflux or ulcers.
medicines.rozad-100: A handwritten brand name in this prescription. Confirm the active ingredient and dose with the prescriber or pharmacist.
medicines.ambulax: A handwritten brand name in this prescription. Confirm the active ingredient and dose with the prescriber or pharmacist.
medicines.pathil plus: A handwritten brand name in this prescription. Confirm the active ingredient and dose with the prescriber or pharmacist.
medicines.placed: A handwritten brand name in this prescription. Confirm the active ingredient and dose with the prescriber or pharmacist.
medicines.eropet 40: A handwritten brand name in this prescription. Confirm the active ingredient and dose with the prescriber or pharmacist.
medicines.dolomi plus: A medicine typically containing paracetamol used for fever and pain relief.
medicines.cetzine: Cetirizine — an antihistamine commonly used to relieve allergy, cold, and sneezing symptoms.
medicines.darochlora: A brand name in this prescription. Confirm the exact medicine and dose with your doctor or pharmacist.
medicines.moxidane: A brand name in this prescription. Confirm the exact medicine and dose with your doctor or pharmacist.
medicines.pantokid: A brand name containing pantoprazole used to reduce stomach acid.
medicines.electrolyte powder: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) / electrolyte powder used to restore hydration and electrolytes lost during illness.

lab_terms.hba1c: A test showing your average blood sugar level over the past 2-3 months.
lab_terms.creatinine: A waste product filtered by your kidneys — high levels can mean your kidneys aren't filtering well.
lab_terms.hemoglobin: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around your body.
lab_terms.ldl: 'Bad' cholesterol — high levels can build up in your arteries.
lab_terms.hdl: 'Good' cholesterol — helps remove bad cholesterol from your blood.
lab_terms.tsh: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone — tells your thyroid gland how much hormone to make.
lab_terms.wbc count: White Blood Cell count — measures cells that fight infection.
lab_terms.platelet count: Measures cells in your blood that help it clot and stop bleeding.
lab_terms.bilirubin: A substance made when red blood cells break down — high levels can indicate liver issues.
lab_terms.esr: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate — a test that can show inflammation somewhere in the body.
lab_terms.bp: Blood pressure — the force of blood moving through your blood vessels.
lab_terms.bmi: Body Mass Index — a screening measure comparing weight with height.
lab_terms.ecg: Electrocardiogram — a test that records the heart's electrical activity.
lab_terms.cbc: Complete Blood Count — a group of tests measuring blood cells.
lab_terms.sgpt: Serum Glutamic Pyruvic Transaminase (ALT) — an enzyme found mainly in the liver.
lab_terms.sgot: Serum Glutamic Oxaloacetic Transaminase (AST) — an enzyme found in liver and heart tissues.
lab_terms.alt: Alanine Aminotransferase — an enzyme that helps check for liver injury.
lab_terms.ast: Aspartate Aminotransferase — an enzyme used alongside ALT to evaluate liver health.
lab_terms.urea: A waste product formed in the liver and eliminated by the kidneys.
lab_terms.bun: Blood Urea Nitrogen — measures the amount of nitrogen in blood from waste product urea.
lab_terms.uric acid: A chemical produced when your body breaks down foods containing purines.
lab_terms.rbc: Red Blood Cell count — indicates the volume of oxygen-carrying cells.
lab_terms.glucose: Blood sugar — the main source of energy for your body's cells.

foods_to_eat: Regular balanced meals with vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein
Drink water and avoid skipping meals
foods_to_avoid: Excess caffeine (coffee, energy drinks, or strong tea) if it worsens anxiety
Alcohol or calming supplements unless your clinician approves them
recommended_exercise: Brisk walking or another comfortable activity, starting gradually
Gentle stretching, yoga, or breathing exercises for relaxation
anxiety.exercise_precautions: Stop activity and seek medical advice for chest pain, fainting, or unusual shortness of breath. New or severe symptoms should be discussed with a clinician.

foods_to_eat: Oats and other whole grains, if tolerated
Yogurt or other probiotic-rich foods, if tolerated
Lean proteins such as chicken or fish
Fresh fruits and vegetables that do not trigger symptoms
foods_to_avoid: Spicy or fried foods if they worsen your symptoms
Caffeine or alcohol if they worsen your symptoms
Large meals close to bedtime if they worsen reflux
recommended_exercise: Gentle walking for 20-30 minutes, as tolerated
Avoid vigorous activity immediately after eating
gastric.exercise_precautions: Food triggers vary. Avoid only foods that worsen your symptoms, and ask your clinician about persistent stomach discomfort.

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens (spinach, kale) rich in potassium
Berries (blueberries, strawberries) high in flavonoids
Oats and whole grains
Bananas, avocados, and garlic
foods_to_avoid: High-sodium processed foods and table salt
Canned soups and salty snacks
Red meat and high-saturated-fat dairy
Excessive caffeine and sugary beverages
recommended_exercise: 30 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise (brisk walking, cycling, or swimming) 5 days a week
Light resistance or weight training 2 days a week
hypertension.exercise_precautions: Avoid sudden heavy weightlifting that causes intense straining.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables (broccoli, asparagus, peppers)
High-fiber foods (beans, lentils, chia seeds)
Lean proteins (chicken breast, fish, tofu)
Complex carbs with low glycemic index (quinoa, brown rice)
foods_to_avoid: Refined sugars, candy, and pastries
Sugary sodas and fruit juices
White bread, white rice, and refined flour products
Deep-fried foods and trans fats
recommended_exercise: 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise (walking, water aerobics)
Post-meal 10-15 minute short walks to help lower glucose spikes
diabetes mellitus.exercise_precautions: Check blood sugar before intense workouts and carry a fast-acting carb source.

foods_to_eat: Fiber-rich vegetables and legumes to stabilize blood glucose
Whole, unprocessed grains and seeds
foods_to_avoid: Simple carbohydrates and added sugars
Processed snacks and sweetened drinks
recommended_exercise: Regular daily walking or moderate cardiovascular exercise to improve insulin sensitivity
hba1c.exercise_precautions: Stay hydrated and monitor blood sugar levels.

foods_to_eat: Soluble fiber foods (oatmeal, kidney beans, Brussels sprouts)
Omega-3 rich foods (salmon, mackerel, walnuts, flaxseeds)
Olive oil and avocados
foods_to_avoid: Saturated fats (butter, lard, full-fat cheese)
Trans fats and commercially baked goods
Organ meats and high-cholesterol processed meats
recommended_exercise: At least 30 minutes of aerobic exercise (brisk walking, jogging, cycling) 5 times a week to boost HDL ('good' cholesterol)
hyperlipidemia.exercise_precautions: Build intensity gradually if new to cardiovascular exercise.

foods_to_eat: Oats, barley, apples, and almonds to lower bad cholesterol
Plant sterol-enriched foods and olive oil
foods_to_avoid: Fried foods, palm oil, butter, and processed meats
recommended_exercise: Brisk walking, jogging, or cycling for 30-45 minutes regularly
ldl.exercise_precautions: Maintain consistency for best lipid-lowering results.

foods_to_eat: Iron-rich foods (spinach, lentils, beans, fortified cereals, lean red meat)
Vitamin C rich foods (citrus fruits, bell peppers) to boost iron absorption
foods_to_avoid: Drinking tea or coffee directly with meals (tannins reduce iron absorption)
Excessive calcium supplements right alongside iron-rich meals
recommended_exercise: Low-to-moderate intensity activities like walking, yoga, and gentle stretching
anemia.exercise_precautions: Rest whenever feeling dizzy or fatigued; avoid overexertion until iron levels normalize.

foods_to_eat: Dark leafy greens, beetroot, dates, raisins, and iron-fortified foods
Oranges and strawberries to enhance iron absorption
foods_to_avoid: Calcium-rich foods at the exact same time as iron foods
recommended_exercise: Light physical activity like walking or restorative yoga
hemoglobin.exercise_precautions: Listen to your body and avoid exhaustion.

foods_to_eat: Kidney-friendly proteins (egg whites, fish, poultry in moderate portions)
Lower-potassium fruits (apples, berries, grapes) if advised by doctor
Cauliflower, cabbage, and red bell peppers
foods_to_avoid: High-sodium foods and added salt
Processed meats and foods with added phosphorus additives
High-potassium foods (bananas, oranges, potatoes) if restricted
recommended_exercise: Gentle aerobic exercise (walking, stationary cycling, light stretching) 3-4 days a week
chronic kidney disease.exercise_precautions: Consult your nephrologist before starting new routines, avoid heavy straining.

foods_to_eat: Plant-based protein sources, fresh vegetables, and adequate water
foods_to_avoid: Excessive cooked red meat (contains cooked creatine)
Creatine supplements and high-sodium meals
recommended_exercise: Moderate, regular activity like walking or light cycling
creatinine.exercise_precautions: Avoid extreme strenuous physical exertion right before lab tests.

foods_to_eat: Anti-inflammatory foods (fatty fish, olive oil, cherries, green tea)
Calcium and Vitamin D rich foods (fortified milk, leafy greens)
foods_to_avoid: Refined sugars and fried foods that promote systemic inflammation
Excessive alcohol
recommended_exercise: Low-impact joint-friendly exercises (swimming, water aerobics, cycling, walking)
Strength training to support muscles around joints
osteoarthritis.exercise_precautions: Avoid high-impact pounding exercises (like running on hard pavement) if joint pain flares up.

foods_to_eat: Selenium-rich foods (Brazil nuts, eggs, legumes)
Iodine and zinc-containing balanced meals
High-fiber foods to aid digestion
foods_to_avoid: Excess raw cruciferous vegetables (cabbage, broccoli) in very large quantities
Highly processed foods and soy right when taking thyroid medication
recommended_exercise: Low-impact aerobic exercise combined with strength training to boost metabolism

foods_to_eat: Heart-healthy Mediterranean diet (olive oil, fish, vegetables, berries)
High-fiber whole grains (oatmeal, brown rice)
foods_to_avoid: High-saturated fats, trans fats, and fried foods
Sodium/salt and processed meats
Sugary drinks and alcohol
recommended_exercise: Physician-supervised cardiac rehabilitation program
Light walking (10-15 minutes daily) gradually increasing as approved by doctor
myocardial infarction.exercise_precautions: CRITICAL: Stop exercise immediately if experiencing chest tightness, breathlessness, or dizziness.

foods_to_eat: Warm fluids (broths, herbal teas, warm water with lemon) for hydration
Protein-dense foods (eggs, poultry, yogurt) to repair tissue
Vitamin C rich fruits (oranges, berries, kiwi)
foods_to_avoid: Cold dairy products if they increase mucus sensation
Processed foods, heavy fried foods, and refined sugar
recommended_exercise: Deep breathing exercises (diaphragmatic breathing) and light indoor walking
Adequate rest — avoid moderate/strenuous exercise while recovering
pneumonia.exercise_precautions: Avoid heavy physical exertion until lung infection and fever have completely cleared.

foods_to_eat: Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage)
Calcium and Vitamin D rich foods
Healthy fats (nuts, seeds, olive oil)
foods_to_avoid: Excessive iodine (seaweed, kelp, iodized salt in large amounts)
Caffeine, energy drinks, and stimulants
Excessive gluten if sensitive
recommended_exercise: Weight-bearing exercises (walking, bodyweight squats) to preserve bone density
Calming exercises like yoga or Pilates
hyperthyroidism.exercise_precautions: Monitor heart rate and avoid strenuous workouts if experiencing tachycardia (fast heart rate).

foods_to_eat: Healthy fats (avocados, olive oil, almonds, walnuts)
Fatty fish rich in Omega-3 (salmon, mackerel, sardines)
High-fiber beans and legumes
foods_to_avoid: Trans fats and hydrogenated oils
Refined carbohydrates and sugary snacks
recommended_exercise: Vigorous or moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, running, swimming) for 30 minutes 5 days a week
hdl.exercise_precautions: Consistency is key to elevating good HDL cholesterol levels.

foods_to_eat: Balanced whole food meals with adequate selenium, zinc, and iodine
foods_to_avoid: Highly processed foods, excessive soy, and caffeine near medication time
recommended_exercise: 30 minutes of regular moderate exercise (walking, cycling) to support metabolic health
tsh.exercise_precautions: Adjust exercise intensity based on current energy and thyroid hormone levels.

foods_to_eat: Immune-supporting foods rich in Vitamin C, zinc, and antioxidants (citrus, garlic, ginger, spinach, yogurt)
foods_to_avoid: Raw or undercooked meats/eggs (to prevent infection risk if WBC is low)
Unpasteurized dairy and unwashed raw produce
recommended_exercise: Light to moderate physical activity (daily walking, stretching)
wbc count.exercise_precautions: Avoid overcrowded public spaces or intense workouts during active infection or low immune status.

foods_to_eat: Folate-rich foods (dark leafy greens, lentils, oranges)
Vitamin K rich foods (kale, spinach, broccoli) if advised by physician
foods_to_avoid: Alcohol and tonic water (quinine can affect platelets)
Excessive cranberry juice or omega-3 megadoses without doctor advice
recommended_exercise: Low-impact non-contact activities (walking, swimming, light elliptical)
platelet count.exercise_precautions: Avoid high-contact sports or activities with high risk of bruising/bleeding if platelets are low.

foods_to_eat: Hydrating fluids, high-fiber fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
Lean protein (poultry, tofu, white fish)
foods_to_avoid: Alcohol completely
High-fat, fried, and heavily spiced foods that strain the liver
recommended_exercise: Light physical activity like short walks and gentle stretching
bilirubin.exercise_precautions: Rest adequately and avoid strenuous exercise if experiencing fatigue or liver inflammation.

foods_to_eat: Anti-inflammatory diet (berries, leafy greens, fatty fish, turmeric, ginger, walnuts)
foods_to_avoid: Refined sugars, fried foods, processed red meats, and artificial additives
recommended_exercise: Low-impact exercise like swimming, water aerobics, or walking to reduce inflammation
esr.exercise_precautions: Do not overexert during acute inflammation flare-ups.

foods_to_eat: Non-starchy vegetables (spinach, broccoli, cauliflower, bell peppers) to help stabilize glucose
High-fiber complex carbohydrates (steel-cut oats, quinoa, lentils, chickpeas)
Lean proteins (skinless poultry, wild fish, tofu, eggs) to promote prolonged satiety
Healthy fats and seeds (chia seeds, ground flaxseeds, raw almonds, avocado)
foods_to_avoid: Sugar-sweetened beverages (sodas, sweetened iced teas, fruit juice concentrates)
Refined carbohydrates (white bread, bakery sweets, refined breakfast cereals)
Ultra-processed snacks with hidden high-fructose corn syrup
recommended_exercise: 10 to 15-minute gentle walk immediately after meals to stimulate muscular glucose uptake
150 minutes per week of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling, or swimming)
Light resistance or bodyweight training 2 times a week to improve insulin sensitivity
glucose.exercise_precautions: Stay well-hydrated. If taking blood sugar-lowering medications, be aware of hypoglycemic symptoms and carry a fast-acting carbohydrate.

foods_to_eat: Plentiful hydration (drink at least 2.5 to 3 liters of water daily to support kidney uric acid excretion)
Low-fat or skim milk and yogurt (dairy proteins help accelerate uric acid clearance)
Tart cherries or fresh berries (contain anthocyanins that help reduce uric acid levels)
Vitamin C-rich fruits and vegetables (oranges, kiwi, bell peppers)
Plant proteins like tofu, lentils, and beans in place of red meat
foods_to_avoid: High-purine animal meats (organ meats like liver/kidneys, beef, lamb, pork)
Purine-dense seafood (anchovies, sardines, mussels, scallops, tuna)
Alcoholic beverages, particularly beer (high purine & brewer's yeast) and hard liquor
Sodas and processed foods sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup
recommended_exercise: Low-impact non-weight-bearing exercises (swimming, stationary cycling, gentle walking) to keep joints mobile
uric acid.exercise_precautions: During an acute gout or joint pain flare, completely rest the affected joint and avoid impact exercises until pain and inflammation subside.

foods_to_eat: Fatty fish rich in Omega-3 fatty acids (salmon, mackerel, sardines) twice weekly
High-fiber whole grains (oats, barley) and legumes
Healthy unsaturated cooking oils (extra virgin olive oil, avocado oil)
Nuts like walnuts and almonds in moderate portion sizes
foods_to_avoid: Alcoholic beverages (even modest alcohol intake can substantially elevate triglyceride levels)
Added refined sugars, candy, pastries, and sweet desserts
Trans fats, hydrogenated shortening, and commercial fried foods
recommended_exercise: At least 30 minutes of moderate-to-brisk aerobic physical activity (brisk walking, jogging, lap swimming) 5 days a week
triglycerides.exercise_precautions: Consistency over weeks and months is key for metabolic triglyceride reduction.

foods_to_eat: Mediterranean dietary pattern: plentiful leafy vegetables, legumes, olive oil, and nuts
Antioxidant-rich foods (berries, green tea, dark leafy greens)
Black or unsweetened coffee (compounds in coffee have been clinically shown to support liver enzyme health)
Lean, unprocessed proteins (fish, skinless chicken, plant proteins)
foods_to_avoid: Alcohol completely to relieve hepatic metabolic stress
High-fructose corn syrup, fruit juices, and table sugars
Deep-fried, ultra-processed, and high-saturated-fat convenience meals
recommended_exercise: 150–200 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise per week combined with moderate resistance training
fatty liver.exercise_precautions: Aim for gradual, sustainable weight management (0.5 to 1 kg per week); avoid rapid crash starvation diets which can worsen hepatic inflammation.

foods_to_eat: Fatty fish (wild salmon, trout, canned sardines)
Vitamin D-fortified milk, fortified plant milks, and fortified cereals
Egg yolks and UV-exposed mushrooms
foods_to_avoid: Excessive alcohol or extreme caffeine intake which can impair calcium/bone balance
recommended_exercise: Weight-bearing exercises (brisk walking, jogging, bodyweight squats, stair climbing) outdoors during safe sunlight hours to stimulate bone mineralization
vitamin d.exercise_precautions: Consult your physician for optimal Vitamin D3 supplementation dosage based on your specific lab result.

foods_to_eat: Dairy products (milk, yogurt, cottage cheese), eggs, and lean poultry
Fortified nutritional yeast and B12-fortified plant-based milks
Fish and seafood (salmon, trout, clams)
foods_to_avoid: Heavy alcohol consumption which interferes with stomach intrinsic factor and B12 absorption
recommended_exercise: Balance and neuromotor exercises (tai chi, yoga, tandem balance walks) to preserve nerve function and stability
vitamin b12.exercise_precautions: Rest if feeling dizzy or uncoordinated; discuss oral or sublingual B12 supplementation with your clinician.

foods_to_eat: Oatmeal and non-citrus fruits (bananas, melons, apples, pears)
Lean poultry (skinless chicken/turkey baked or grilled) and seafood
Green vegetables (asparagus, broccoli, green beans, celery, cucumbers)
Herbal teas such as chamomile or licorice root
foods_to_avoid: Citrus fruits (oranges, lemons, grapefruits) and tomato-based sauces
Chocolate, peppermint, and spearmint (relax the lower esophageal sphincter)
Caffeine, carbonated fizzy beverages, and alcohol
High-fat fried foods and eating within 3 hours of bedtime
recommended_exercise: Low-impact upright activities like walking or light stationary cycling
gerd.exercise_precautions: Avoid intense forward bending, inverted yoga poses, or vigorous abdominal crunches right after meals; stay upright for 2 to 3 hours after eating.
